history.heading: Dacia and Rome
paragraphs: In antiquity, the lands of present-day Romania were home to the Dacians, who built a powerful kingdom under Burebista and Decebalus. The Roman Emperor Trajan conquered Dacia in 106 CE, and Roman settlement shaped the Romanian language, which descends from Latin.

After the Romans withdrew, many peoples passed through the region. In the Middle Ages the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia formed in the 14th century, while Transylvania was part of the Kingdom of Hungary.

history.heading: Princes and empires
paragraphs: The principalities resisted Ottoman expansion under rulers such as Stephen the Great of Moldavia and Vlad III "the Impaler" of Wallachia, the inspiration for Dracula, before becoming Ottoman vassals. Michael the Brave briefly united the three regions in 1600.

Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859 under Alexandru Ioan Cuza, forming Romania, which became independent in 1878 and a kingdom in 1881. After the First World War, Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina joined in 1918, creating Greater Romania.

history.heading: War and communism
paragraphs: In the Second World War, Romania allied with Nazi Germany under Ion Antonescu, and hundreds of thousands of Jews and Roma were killed. In 1944 it switched sides. A communist regime took power, and Nicolae Ceaușescu, ruler from 1965, built a harsh personality cult and imposed severe austerity.

The 1989 revolution was the only violent overthrow of a communist regime in Eastern Europe; Ceaușescu was executed. Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007. In 2024 the presidential election was annulled over alleged Russian interference, and pro-European Nicușor Dan won the rerun in 2025.

culture.heading: Language and faith
paragraphs: Romanian is a Romance language, related to Italian, French and Spanish. Most Romanians are Orthodox Christians, and there are significant Hungarian (mainly in Transylvania) and Roma minorities. The painted monasteries of Bukovina and the wooden churches of Maramureș are UNESCO sites.
Writers include the national poet Mihai Eminescu and Eugène Ionesco; sculptor Constantin Brâncuși was a pioneer of modern art.

culture.heading: Traditions and food
paragraphs: Mărțișor, celebrating spring, and the Călușari dance are recognised by UNESCO. Food includes sarmale (cabbage rolls), mămăligă (polenta) and mici (grilled sausages). Gymnast Nadia Comăneci scored the first perfect 10 at the 1976 Olympics. The Carpathian Mountains and Danube Delta are natural treasures.

politics.heading: Semi-presidential republic
paragraphs: Romania is a semi-presidential republic. The president, elected for five years, has significant powers in foreign and defence policy, while the prime minister leads the government. Fighting corruption has been a major theme. Romania is a member of the EU and NATO, joined Schengen fully in 2025, and hosts NATO forces and a US missile defence site.

economy.heading: Fast-growing economy
paragraphs: Romania's economy has grown strongly since EU accession. Key sectors include car manufacturing (Dacia, owned by Renault, and Ford), IT and outsourcing, agriculture, energy (including natural gas in the Black Sea) and services. Bucharest and Cluj-Napoca are tech hubs.
Romania uses the leu. It faces a large budget deficit, regional inequality, and emigration, with millions of Romanians working elsewhere in Europe.
